title: Digital finance is widening access while scams, wallets, payment products, and complaint routing become central consumer-protection risks
geography: Financial consumer-protection authorities and financial-services markets across 60 jurisdictions, including banking, payments, credit, insurance, investment, and pensions

denominator.unit: jurisdictions represented by 107 government ministries and financial authorities in the OECD reporting exercise

top_operating_environment_risk.unit: risk ranked highest by responding authorities for financial consumers in 2025

low_middle_income_scam_risk_share.unit: percent of low- and middle-income jurisdiction responses identifying financial scams and frauds as a significant operating-environment risk

high_income_scam_risk_share.unit: percent of high-income jurisdiction responses identifying financial scams and frauds as a significant operating-environment risk

risk_categories.value: operating environment, consumer demand-side circumstances, provider conduct, product sectors, scams/frauds, and complaints

observations.method: OECD synthesis of a reporting template completed by financial consumer-protection ministries, regulators, and authorities, supplemented by secondary sources.
observations.uncertainty: The exercise captures authority assessments and selected secondary indicators, not a population prevalence estimate, consumer-level incidence rate, causal effect, or comparable administrative total across countries.
observations.subgroup: Financial consumer-protection authorities, banks, payment providers, insurers, credit firms, investment and pension providers, consumers, and vulnerable or digitally exposed groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher authority attention can reflect stronger detection, reporting, and regulatory capacity rather than a uniformly higher underlying harm rate.

observations.period: 2025; digital payments, scams, and fraud mechanisms

denominator.unit: jurisdiction responses identifying significant scam or fraud types by number of people affected

phishing_vishing_smishing.unit: percent of applicable responses selecting phishing, vishing, or smishing for personal information among significant fraud types by people affected

provider_impersonation.unit: percent selecting fraudsters posing as banks, advisers, or financial providers among significant fraud types by people affected

fake_payment_insurance_schemes.unit: percent selecting fake payment, investment, or insurance schemes among significant fraud types by people affected

digital_payment_scale.unit: US dollars projected total digital-payment transaction value in 2026, more than

reported_consumer_losses.unit: US dollars in estimated consumer losses from financial scams and frauds in 2025

observations.method: OECD classification of fraud types and synthesis of authority-reported risk patterns, with secondary estimates for global digital-payment value and losses.
observations.uncertainty: The percentages describe authority selections, while the loss estimate is secondary and not a harmonized administrative count; neither establishes individual exposure, recovery, or causality.
observations.subgroup: Users of mobile banking, digital wallets, cards, push payments, cross-border transactions, and online financial platforms; providers, platforms, telecoms, and law enforcement.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital channels can reduce access costs and expand inclusion; stronger authentication, reporting, and cross-sector controls can reduce harm without restricting legitimate use.

observations.period: 2025-2026; product-level detriment and unequal digital-finance exposure

denominator.unit: jurisdiction responses assessing banking and payment products giving rise to consumer detriment

mobile_banking_top_three.unit: percent of applicable responses selecting mobile banking among the top three banking/payment products causing detriment in 2025

transaction_accounts_top_three.unit: percent selecting transaction accounts among the top three banking/payment products causing detriment in 2025

digital_wallet_top_three.unit: percent selecting digital wallets among the top three banking/payment products causing detriment in 2025

debit_card_top_three.unit: percent selecting debit cards among the top three banking/payment products causing detriment in 2025

low_middle_income_mobile_banking.unit: percent selecting mobile banking in low- and middle-income jurisdictions versus 44 percent in high-income jurisdictions

low_middle_income_wallet_debit.unit: percent selecting each of digital wallets and debit cards in low- and middle-income jurisdictions versus 22 percent in high-income jurisdictions

observations.method: OECD comparison of authority assessments by financial-product sector and jurisdiction income group.
observations.uncertainty: Product rankings reflect domestic authority judgment and selected response denominators; they do not establish consumer-level harm, product quality, or a universal income-gradient mechanism.
observations.subgroup: High-income and low- or middle-income jurisdictions, mobile-banking users, wallet and debit-card users, providers, and supervisors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher concern in lower-income markets may reflect faster product expansion, different reporting capacity, or product mix rather than greater harm per user.

observations.period: 2024-2025; complaint routing, redress, and supervisory visibility

denominator.unit: jurisdiction responses reporting trends in complaints received by supervisory authorities from 2024 to 2025

supervisory_complaint_increase.unit: percent of reporting jurisdictions indicating higher complaint volumes received by supervisory authorities from 2024 to 2025, approximately

firm_or_adr_complaint_increase.unit: percent of reporting jurisdictions indicating higher total complaint volumes received by firms or alternative-dispute-resolution schemes from 2024 to 2025, approximately

banking_complaint_subject.value: scams and frauds were the most common subject across firms, ADR schemes, and supervisory authorities

complaint_boundary.value: more complaints may mean more harm, better awareness, greater confidence in redress, or improved reporting

observations.method: OECD comparison of aggregate complaint-volume direction and complaint subjects across firms, alternative dispute-resolution schemes, and supervisory authorities.
observations.uncertainty: Complaint data are not representative of all consumers; routing, reporting, awareness, and institutional confidence affect observed volumes, and complaint receipt does not prove remedy, adequacy, or recovery.
observations.subgroup: Consumers who complain, firms, ADR schemes, supervisory authorities, financial products, and people who do not or cannot use complaint channels.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rise in complaints directed to supervisors can indicate stronger institutional visibility and recourse rather than worsening product conduct alone.

related_sources.claim: OECD publication identifier for Consumer Finance Risk Monitor 2026.
Related OECD report on fraud drivers, typology, protection, redress, reporting, literacy, and anti-fraud collaboration.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-finance market-to-protection route linking digital payments, fraud, product design, unequal exposure, complaint routing, supervision, and redress visibility. In this source, respondents are public authorities and ministries, not individual consumers; the record is not respondent-level household data, individual victimization, causal loss, completed remedy, or proof that complaint increases mean worsening harm.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD Consumer Finance Risk Monitor 2026 PDF was reviewed; jurisdiction and authority methodology, scam risk, fraud typology, digital-payment exposure, product detriment, income-group contrasts, complaint routing, and interpretation boundaries were cross-checked.
